summary: This standards-track memo defines a Management Information Base module for Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation (MAP-E), for use with network management protocols such as SNMP. It lets MAP-E devices be monitored and managed in a standard way.

plainLanguage.summary: A dashboard for a special tunnel system. It defines the standard dials and counters so any tool can read how the system is doing.

questions: how to monitor map-e with snmp
what is a basic mapping rule
is the map-e mib read only
subtitle: A standard set of read-only SNMP counters and tables for watching MAP-E tunnels, which carry IPv4 over an IPv6 network.

tldr.problem: MAP-E gives users IPv4 connectivity over a provider's IPv6 network, but operators had no standard way to monitor MAP-E devices through network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module, MAP-E-MIB, with a table of mapping rules and a table of counters for packets that fail MAP security checks. Both are indexed per tunnel interface.
tldr.outcome: Every object is read-only, so the module is for monitoring, not configuring. Devices that implement it must support both its rule group and its security group.

today: RFC 8389 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the MAP-E MIB for monitoring RFC 7597 devices.

sections.title: What the MAP-E MIB Is For
sections.content:
Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation (MAP-E, RFC 7597) is a stateless, automatic tunneling mechanism. It provides an IPv4 connectivity service to end users over a service provider's IPv6 network.

RFC 8389 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring MAP-E devices. MIB objects are generally read through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and this module is written in SMIv2, the Structure of Management Information.
sections.plainLanguage: MAP-E is a secret passage that lets old-style mail travel through a new kind of road. This document lists the gauges you can read to see how the passage is doing.

sections.title: How the Module Is Organized
sections.content:
The IF-MIB (RFC 2863) defines generic managed objects for interfaces. Each tunnel is handled as a logical interface with its own ifEntry, and each MAP-E tunnel endpoint acts as a virtual interface with a matching entry in the IF-MIB. Entries are indexed by ifIndex, so the MAP-E MIB is configurable per interface and depends on the IF-MIB.

The module has two object subtrees plus a conformance subtree. It is registered at mib-2 242.

  • mapRule: the managed objects for the multiple mapping rules in MAP-E.
  • mapSecurityCheck: statistics on invalid packets that were identified.
  • mapMIBConformance: conformance information.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tunnel end has its own card in a filing cabinet. The MAP-E gauges are filed behind that card, in one drawer for rules and one for suspicious mail.

sections.title: The Mapping Rule Table
sections.content:
The rule table is indexed by ifIndex and mapRuleID, a unique identifier that distinguishes rules. Each entry describes one mapping rule with these read-only objects.

  • mapRuleIPv6Prefix and mapRuleIPv6PrefixLen: the IPv6 prefix and its length, as assigned to CEs.
  • mapRuleIPv4Prefix and mapRuleIPv4PrefixLen: the IPv4 prefix and its length.
  • mapRuleBRIPv6Address: the IPv6 address of the Border Relay (BR) conveyed to CEs.
  • mapRulePSID and mapRulePSIDLen: the Port Set ID, which algorithmically identifies a set of ports assigned to a CE, and its bit length (0 to 16).
  • mapRuleOffset: 0 to 15, with a default of 6 to exclude the system ports (0-1023).
  • mapRuleEALen: the length of the Embedded Address, 0 to 48.
  • mapRuleType: the kind of rule.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule is a recipe card. It says which address block belongs to whom, which exit door to use, and which slice of port numbers each customer gets.

sections.title: Rule Types: BMR and FMR
sections.content:
Per RFC 7597, mapping rules are either a Basic Mapping Rule (BMR) or a Forwarding Mapping Rule (FMR). Under RFC 7598, an F-flag says whether a rule is used for forwarding. If it is set, the rule is an FMR. If not, the rule is BMR only and MUST NOT be used for forwarding.

A BMR can also serve as an FMR when the F-flag is set, so the RuleType textual convention has three values: bmr(1), fmr(2) and bmrAndfmr(3). The third covers a BMR that is also an FMR, for mesh mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Some rules only tell you how to build your own address. Others also say how to send mail onward. A rule can do one job or both, and the MIB records which.

sections.title: Security Check Counters
sections.content:
The mapSecurityCheck subtree counts invalid packets, of the two kinds RFC 7597 defines.

  • The Border Relay validates a received packet's source IPv6 address against the configured MAP domain rule, and its destination IPv6 address against the configured BR IPv6 address.
  • A MAP node (CE or BR) checks that a received packet's source IPv4 address and port fall in the range derived from the matching MAP rule.

Two Counter64 objects hold the results: mapSecurityCheckInvalidv4 and mapSecurityCheckInvalidv6.
sections.plainLanguage: A guard at the door checks each letter's return address. The guard keeps a tally of how many letters had a fake or wrong one.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content: The compliance statement lists two mandatory groups: mapMIBRuleGroup for the mapping rule objects and mapMIBSecurityGroup for the two security counters. An implementation that claims conformance supports both.
sections.plainLanguage: To get the badge, a device must offer both the rules page and the guard's tally page.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this module has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. If the module is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot alter or create its objects through SNMP SET operations.

Some objects may still be sensitive in some environments, because the information they hold may help target an attack. The RFC lists the rule table's prefix, PSID, offset, EA length and type objects. It says it is important to control even GET and NOTIFY access, and possibly to encrypt values sent over SNMP. It recommends SNMPv3 with the User-based Security Model for authentication and privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: You can look at the gauges but not turn the knobs. Even so, who gets to look should be controlled, because the readings could help a bad guy.
